utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis, along with Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Representing Mico Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, Miroslav Cuskic, and Eelke Daatselaar appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any housekeeping matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly. Yesterday there was an oral ruling concerning the Prosecution's motion to reopen its case. I was asked to seek a clarification. The final point, I think, Judge Harhoff mentioned was we ask the Prosecution to provide us with at least a template translation of the documents. And I wanted to clarify: Is that just for the death certificates or for all of the documents, autopsy reports, and others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To the extent in which it is possible to have template translations made also for the other documents, we would like to have that. I believe that the template translations is a term of art invented by the Prosecution itself, so you know better than anyone else what a template translation is. And I think that at the previous occasion you did provide such translations also for the other documents, that is to say, the -- the death certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- the death certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I suspected that was the intention. I wanted to clarify that basically those documents that lend themselves to a template translation is that -- those that are basically a form where it's filled in with a name and a date, et cetera. So we will do that, Your Honours. That's all I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go into closed session so the witness can be escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: (redacted

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness you should have on the monitor Exhibit P539, which is, as I said, apparently a brief news report of a press conference. And with Mr. Zupljanin who apparently said a little more than halfway through: "All employees must sign the text of the formal declaration by 15 April, and if they fail to do that, their employment will cease." Doesn't that indicate that, whether that was his personal position or the position of the Law on Internal Affairs or the minister of internal affairs and/or the Crisis Staff of Banja Luka or the autonomous region, Mr. Zupljanin was supporting it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've said, the signing of solemn declarations, and this also mentions new uniforms with insignia, to my mind, was a decision, possibly of the Assembly of the ARK or of the Crisis Staff, and Mr. Zupljanin only related the instructions an orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was only following orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in this case he informed the public that solemn declarations would be signed and that uniforms would be changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, according to you, whose orders was he following when he informed about that deadline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, I don't know much about politics and I've never meddled much, but possibly the Autonomous Region of Krajina; that is, its assembly. But I really can't tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, don't you, though, that Mr. Zupljanin was a member of the Crisis Staff of the ARK, the Autonomous Region of the Krajina. You were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that, by virtue of his position as chief of the CSB, he was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you, next, exhibit 1D138. This is tab is 13 of the Prosecution's list. This one will be on your screen in a minute, Witness. I'll tell you, it's from Minister Delimustafic, dated the 10th of April, to all CSBs and SJBs. Well, let me ask you first: Did you ever see this or were you aware of this document in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you read there that Mr. Delimustafic is referring to what he calls the so-called Serbian MUP being in progress of forming organisational units. And he says that what was happening was that some employees were being pressured and blackmailed, especially non-Serbs, to sign some sort of what he calls "declarations of loyalty. Otherwise, their employment will allegedly be terminated?" That's an accurate description, isn't it, that if people didn't sign those declarations they were going to be and, indeed, were terminated? Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have said earlier that any staff who did not sign the solemn declaration, that their employment was terminated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at the number at the top of that dispatch. You'll see it's number 09/4-382. If you remember that for a second. And let me show you the next exhibit, which is Prosecution tab 14. The exhibit number, P354. Do you have that on your screen now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, this is from Mr. Zupljanin on -- also on the 10th of April, and he's making reference to that document we just looked at, 09/4-382, which he refers to as communications about the "forced" formation of organisational units of the Serb MUP. And he says: "We hereby warn you that this is not forced in any way. It's about legal and legitimate organs in the Serb Republic." And then in the next paragraph, the last two sentences say: "They are to sign a formal statement in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serb Republic of BiH. This should be no different from the statement of the ex-minister of internal affairs and should have nothing to do with the so-called statement of loyalty, as was noted in the dispatch ..." From Mr. Delimustafic. And he goes on to say: "This dispatch," I think it refers to Mr. Delimustafic's, "-- doesn't have legal effect in the territory of the Serb republic ... and is being put out of force." Did you see this document? Were you aware of this in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, I'm not sure. I may have; I may not have. But in late April - maybe on the 27th - some laws were adopted; among others, the Law on Internal Affairs of the RS. I'm not sure about this though. I don't know if I ever had a chance to look at it or if I was even informed of it. I may have seen it at the time. Especially since this dispatch, to my mind, focuses on the signing of solemn declarations by CSB staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'll see there's reference that this be done by the 15th of April; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to one more. This is Exhibit P355; tab 15 of the Prosecution's list. You see the first page of the document. This is also dated the 10th of April, 1992. And I would tell you that it comes from Mr. Zupljanin. We'll see the last page in a bit. But it's to various SJB chiefs and to, I guess, chiefs of CSB departments and also to the presidents of certain Serb municipalities about conclusions from the enlarged centre council session held on 6th of April, 1992. First of all, can you tell me, do you know what the centre council was in Banja Luka CSB? Who or what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about the council of the centre. But I suppose that it's the professional collegium. That's what we called it. And I would not know who the members of the council were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take you to, I guess it's page 3 in the B/C/S, and also page 3 of the English. It's item number 3. And my English translation says: "Upon the receipt of their new post assignments, authorised employees will have to sign a solemn declaration, the text of which is identical to that of the solemn declaration from the previous Law on Internal Affairs. The employees were given the deadline of 15 April ... to sign the declaration. Those who fail to sign the declaration by that date will have their employment with the Serbian Republic Ministry of internal affairs terminated." You told us you signed the declaration. And I take it, did you sign it before the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I signed the solemn declaration as soon as the department chief Stevan Markovic gave me the declaration to sign. And I signed in his presence. May have been on the 5th, or the 6th, or the 10th of April. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, did you read the declaration before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you compare the language of the one you signed with the language of the old solemn declaration from the Socialist Republic of BiH MUP to satisfy yourself that it was identical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have the old solemn declaration on me. But the text of the solemn declaration itself, in my opinion, was identical, apart from one part, the previous solemn declarations that I signed as a soldier of the JNA and when taking up employment with the organs of the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I leave this document, if we could go to page 5 in the English. And it's -- yes, it's the last page in B/C/S. Item number 17, Witness, says: "All authorised employees who do not sign the solemn declaration and thus have no intention of remaining in the service shall return ... weapons and equipment ..." Were you aware, did that happen? Did those employees who did not sign have to turn in their weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in all our documents or enactments there's an obligation of MUP employees, in case of leaving the service or retiring or, God forbid, dying - in that case, it's the obligation of their families - to return the relevant items. When I retired, I returned my side-arm and the handcuffs, the baton. So that all staff who, for any reasons, leave the organs of the interior or move on to other related organs must return any items issued to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm having trouble with my transcript. Let me show you, then, another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can look at P510. I believe this is tab 90 in the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is -- Witness, this is the old Socialist Republic of BiH Law on Internal Affairs, and I want to look at Article 41, which has the text of the solemn declaration as it read then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page number 12 in the English, it's ERN P0035097 in the B/C/S, to Article 41.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with the help of the usher, I can hand you a hard copy. Thank you. If you would take a look at that, sir. At the end of Article 41 is the declaration, and in my English translation it says: "I hereby declare that I will perform the duties of an authorised official conscientiously and responsibly, that I will abide by the constitution and the law, that I will protect the constitutional order and the rights, freedoms, and security of working people and citizens with all my strength, and that I will perform these and other duties and tasks of an authorised official even when the performance of such duties and tasks puts my own life at risk." I know it may be asking you a lot to ask you if you remember that's the solemn declaration that you made when you first joined the MUP back in 1979. Do you have any reason to doubt that it was as it's worded here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... then I'd like to have you look at and compare the solemn declaration as it's worded in the new RS Law on Internal Affairs from March of 1992. This is Exhibit P530, tab 91 on the Prosecution list. And I will have the usher hand you a hard copy of this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'll grant you that they're similar but I put it to you that they're not identical. This one says: "I hereby state that I will execute the duties of an authorised official in a conscientious and responsible manner, that I will strictly follow the constitution and laws, that I shall protect with all my strength the constitutionally established order of the republic, rights, freedoms, and security, and that I shall execute these duties and other duties of an authorised official even when my life is in danger." You'll notice there's no reference to rights, freedoms, and security of working people and citizens. So that's one change that's noticeable. You weren't aware of that at the time when you signed your solemn declaration in April of 1992, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, the solemn declaration that I signed in April, to my mind, only differs from the solemn declaration as it was in 1990 when I took up employment. In the sentence mentioning the constitutional order of the republic, and let me tell you, I lived in that republic and it's normal for the solemn declaration to mention the order of the republic. If this were another country, the language would probably be the same: The order of the republic. Meaning the republic where you live. And as for the rights, freedoms, and security, I personally do not see any difference, apart from the order of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... what's missing, at least as I read the English, is there is no reference to working people and citizens in the new one; whereas, they were specifically referred to in the old one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. The new solemn declaration does not include that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: There, it just uses the term "republic," but I think we've seen a couple of declarations that were signed in April 1992 where there was a specific reference to the republic of -- to the Serbian Republic of BiH. Do you recall if that term was on the declaration that you signed? Not just the word "republic," but "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I have just said if it were, let's say, the Republic of Croatia or the Republic of Macedonia, it would also be a republic. But I can't recall clearly, but I'm pretty sure that the language was Republika Srpska, because that is the country where I live. That's my personal understanding. That's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You can set those aside for now. I want to show you Exhibit P470. This is at tab 16 from the Prosecution's list. Witness, this will be on your screen in a moment. It's a newspaper article from Glas, dated the 16th of April, 1992. And it's called -- the headline is: "Preserving peace as a joint concern." I don't know, can you read it there, or is it too small? I can give you a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be easier for you to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is a story about, on the 15th of April, the mayor Mr. Predrag Radic received a delegation from the SDA, and according to Mr. Krzic one of the reasons for this meeting was because of a statement from Mr. Zupljanin that his service was unable to give cast-iron guarantees about the security of citizens' property? Do you see that in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry about that. And if we could go to page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for you, I think I've marked it in a blue highlighter, the paragraph where I want you to look next. It mentions the SDA delegation was seeking a postponement of the application of the Law on Internal Affairs so that Muslims who did not wish to sign a statement of loyalty could remain in the CSB. So this is the 15th, the deadline for signing, the SDA is meeting with the mayor and asking if there could be a postponement. And it says: "The request was rejected." Did you know that? Did you know about that discussion in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of this discussion. I was not aware of it being held in the Banja Luka town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could go on to the next paragraph, I think it's the second sentence. It says: "Bajazit Jahic, chief of public security at the CSB, also spoke at this meeting and said he had stopped working today because he did not wish to sign a statement of loyalty ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me request --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, Witness, I'd like to show you Exhibit 2D018. This is at tab 17 in the Prosecution's list. Sort of going chronologically here, sir, this is a dispatch, number 11-98, dated the 16th of April, 1992 - it should be on your screen in a moment - from the chief. And he's making reference to the extended collegium that was held earlier in the month, where it was decided all authorised officials employed at the CSB Banja Luka should sign a solemn declaration by the 15th of April. In the fourth paragraph, it says: "The obligations mentioned in this telegram do not apply to ... Prijedor and Kotor Varos SJB. Authorised officials at these stations may continue to wear the current insignia if they wish, until further notice." And then in parentheses it says: "(Until the political situation in these municipalities is solved)." Do you know anything about that? Why was there an exception made about signing the solemn declaration and wearing the insignia for Prijedor and Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see from this dispatch that SJBs Prijedor and Kotor Varos are exempted from signing the solemn declaration. The reason for this is the multi-ethnic composition of the SJB in Prijedor and the SJB in Kotor Varos, as well as the multi-ethnic composition of the population in those areas. The majority population there, if you can say it that way, maybe in inverted commas, because there were other nations living there as well. And you can see here that this applied until the resolution of the political situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it a fact that the way that situation was resolved was that the Serbs took over control in Prijedor at the end of April? Isn't that how they resolved the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, no, what it says here is that there's a delay on the deadline until the political situation can be resolved. And my question is: Don't you know that the Serbs took control of Prijedor by taking over all the offices and placing themselves in those positions? And that's how the situation was resolved, and then people in Prijedor had to sign the solemn declaration and start wearing the insignia of the RS MUP, or the Serbian Republic of BiH MUP. That's what happened in Prijedor, right, around the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but there are far too many questions contained in here. I would ask my colleague Mr. Hannis to stop after the first question, whether he is aware, and then to continue with other questions, instead of suggesting answers to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's one of the joys of cross-examination, is to be able to suggest answers to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I misspoke. You have that right, of course. However, I would like you to ask one question first, and then when something is established, to go on suggesting other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't a referendum held to resolve the political situation in Prijedor, was there? They didn't vote on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. Let me then go to Exhibit P560. This is tab 21. And, again, this is a newspaper article. And it may be helpful for you to have a hard copy. Is that easier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is another article from Glas. I think dated the 12th of May 1992. An interview with Chief Zupljanin. And I've marked with a blue highlighter the parts I want to ask you about. In English, it's about ten or 12 lines up from the bottom. You see a part there where it talks about the transformation of the republic? And Mr. Zupljanin is saying: "In this area it went faster than elsewhere ..." Do you find that? I think it's on the lower left of the first column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And there, he says: "It went faster than elsewhere, and it was less painful, because we started preparing for the transformation immediately after the constitution of the Serbian Republic of BH came into force on 23 March of this year, and the internal affairs law on 27 March." Do you recall what kind of preparations Mr. Zupljanin and CSB Banja Luka were taking immediately after the 23rd and the 27 of March to prepare for this transformation? Did you know about any of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In relation to this transformation and the preparations, I only know that the constitution of Republika Srpska was promulgated at the end of March, that a number of laws were enacted. I don't know exactly which laws, but I do know that a new Law on Internal Affairs was enacted. And I know that the constitution and the law contained the provisions stipulating that the people working in internal affairs were to receive new uniforms, with new insignia and new caps. That's all I know. Now as to all these other things, preparations, that's something that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. The next sentence, he mentioned that they've already changed the insignia, and employees who have stayed have signed their solemn declaration. And then he went on to say: "I should say, as I have done [sic] earlier, that this declaration is no different from the declaration ... employees had to ... sign pursuant to the earlier law ..." It seems to me that Mr. Zupljanin has, on several occasions, repeated this, that there is no difference. But we've seen that there are differences. Do you think that's because he knew there was a difference but he didn't want to talk about it? Do you have any idea why he would say that when it's clear that there is a difference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I'm not sure how helpful the witness's answer to that question would be. Because apart from being speculative, it is possible to argue that substantially there's no difference between the two forms of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No substantial difference, Your Honour, but clearly not identical as was asserted. I take your point. I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would go to the next section I've highlighted --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we have to go to page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Mr. Zupljanin is saying in the area of the Serbian Republic of BH there can only be -- there can be only the government of the Serbian people. Thus, the problem of Prijedor has been settled. And this is on the 12th of May, so we know that was settled on about the 30th of April. He mentioned some problems remaining in Jajce and Kotor Varos. He says: "I trust that in a peaceful way we shall have the government taken over by the one who it belongs to." Is he referring to the Serbian people there, as the one to whom the government belongs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read it. I have read the statement by Mr. Zupljanin. I see no elements that I saw when I was signing the solemn declaration. In this specific case, the republic that was mentioned was Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I guess you -- you don't know the answer to my question about who he's referring to there when he says "we shall have the government taken over by the one who it belongs to."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know that. You can interpret it in two different ways, three different ways, even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question on this document, if I may, Your Honour, before the break. In the next paragraph you'll see: "We shall keep the peace if we are carrying out the decisions of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." And one of these is about giving back the weapons. You're aware that around this time there were operations, joint operations, by the police and the military to collect weapons in the Autonomous Region of Krajina; do you know about those operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know about any of the operations in the -- throughout the ARK in -- in almost all of the municipalities, where the police were going to Muslim and Croat villages primarily and searching houses and collecting weapons? You didn't know about that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware that in the Banja Luka town there were paramilitary formations and armed civilians wearing different uniforms. Military police was in charge of paramilitary formations and uniformed individuals. And as for civilians who were armed, it was the organs of internal affairs who were in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We move into closed session so the witness may be escorted out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone of the accused should be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I heard the interpreter say the microphone of the accused should be switched off. So I don't know if there's a microphone on over there somewhere or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just checking on a technical matter, sir. Okay. Now let me talk a little bit -- go back in time a little bit and talk about some of the events leading up to the split of the former socialist MUP and the creation of the Serbian MUP in Bosnia. I'd like to show Exhibit P864. And this is tab 5 of the Prosecution's binder. And, again, it's another newspaper article. I don't know, does it help you to have the hard copies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if it's easier to read than on the screen or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is dated the 5th of March, 1992, from Glas. There are actually two articles I want to ask you about. The first one is about the Krajina government in the offing. And I think that's the one that's at the top of the page with the photograph. I've marked with the blue highlighter the part that I wanted to ask you about. I think it's the third paragraph. It mentions the results of a meeting of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. It said they passed a number of decisions or adopted a number of decisions about the formation of some important government departments, such as the decision about forming a Security Services Centre for the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Did you know about that, that the ARK Assembly had adopted a decision to create a Security Services Centre of its own, apparently, in early March 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of that decision, and it's normal that I should, because I was a member of an organ of the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then I want to ask you about a second article, which my English translation says: "From the press conference of the chief of CSB, Banja Luka, Stojan Zupljanin, peace -- the strategic aim." And I want to go to the very end of the article. My English translation reads: "To a journalist's question whether, in future, the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka would carry out the orders of the BH interior ministry, Zupljanin replied that the centre he was responsible for would not carry out any orders of the Bosnia and Herzegovina interior ministry that might possibly be directed against the interests of the Serbian people." Do you see that? Were you aware that Mr. Zupljanin had made that statement on the 4th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a career policeman. Were you aware of the Law on Internal Affairs in existence at that time, in March 1992? I think that was the version of the law that was passed in January of 1990. You knew basically the provisions of your own Law on Internal Affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I knew some provisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems to me that refusing to obey an order from the minister or the ministry would be in violation of the Law on the Interior, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, for example, if hypothetically speaking, the -- Mr. Delimustafic had issued a decision that from -- from now on all internal memos should be printed on green paper, and Mr. Zupljanin might feel that that was contrary to the interests of the Serbian people, in your opinion, would he be permitted to disobey such a decision, or an order, to use green paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you, next, tab 8 in the Prosecution binder. It's Exhibit 1D137. Again, with the usher's help, I'll hand you a hard copy. It is a dispatch from CSB Banja Luka dated the 3rd of April, 1992. And take a minute, if you want to read through it. I'm not going to ask you about the whole thing. I'm particularly interested in the last -- the next-to-the-last paragraph, where Mr. Zupljanin's talking about the security situation in the last 24 hours. Let me know when you're ready for that question. In that paragraph he says that: "Barricades were erected at the approaches to Banja Luka and in the town itself by members of the Serbian Defence Forces ..." First of all, can you tell me, do you know who the so-called Serbian Defence Forces were in Banja Luka on the 4th of April, 1993, the SOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, as far as I know, the Serbian Defence Forces, SOS, were members of the military, members of the Territorial Defence who were armed, wearing military uniforms. And there were even members of other formations with long-barrelled weapons. They were military reservists and members of the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Help clarify for me, will you: When you say "members of the military," do you mean JNA, or Territorial Defence, active duty or reservists, or both? What exactly do you mean there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by ethnicity, were these Serbs, Muslims, Croats; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this is about Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Zupljanin reports that the SOS presented the Crisis Staff with certain conditions which were accepted after lengthy discussions. "One of those conditions was the application of the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic should begin immediately and solemn declarations signed." Do you know why Serb members of the Territorial Defence would be insisting on application of the Law on Internal Affairs and the signing of solemn declarations? What do they have to do with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, they had nothing to do with the CSB, nor could they influence it. And I heard about these demands. They were allegedly demanding that the Yugoslav People's Army, which, at the time, was withdrawing from the barracks, but they were also along the separation lines where there were armed conflicts. And when they were withdrawing with their weapons and pulling out of the barracks, that may have been the main reason for their fear. Well, maybe not fear. But for their demands that the army place itself in the service of the people. Why one of the conditions should have been that the police should sign solemn declarations under the constitution of the RS and put insignia on their uniforms, well, that may have been because at the time in Banja Luka, and most probably elsewhere too, there were various people - I won't call them formations - but people wearing uniforms with various insignia, various kinds of uniforms, and they were -- they had long-barrelled weapons. And I suppose that the reason was to be able to tell with certainty who was a member of the security services. In other words, the police. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What about these SOS? Did you see them around town at these barricades? And what kind of uniforms were they wearing; if you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I know, I heard of their existence, but I haven't seen them around so I couldn't tell what kind of uniforms they're wearing and with what kind of insignia or who was their leader or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we leave the document, the last page in English and the next-to-the-last paragraph on the last page in B/C/S, Chief Zupljanin again mentions he would like to remind you that the text of the solemn declaration is identical to that of the solemn declaration in the previous law. So, again, we see him mentioning that. SOS, let me show you a couple of more documents about that. Prosecution tab 10; exhibit number P536. And, again, if I could have the assistance of the usher, I'll hand you a hard copy. And this is from the Glas newspaper on Saturday, the 4th of April. Actually, there are a number of articles I want to ask you about, and I've handed you a hard copy of page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to that in the e-court. And the first article is called: The word of the warrior. It talks about the municipal Crisis Staff accepting conditions from the Serbian Defence Forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see that? I think that's the big article at the top of the page with the picture next to it. Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the gentleman in the picture on the top right? Do you recognise any of those guys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second from the right is Mr. Brdjanin, who lived in my neighbourhood, not far from where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can believe me that, on the left and right -- to the left or the right of Mr. Brdjanin there may be the late president of the Banja Luka municipal assembly, Mr. Radic, but I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see in the story that President Radic declared that all the SOS demands had been agreed to, although some in a slightly modified form. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the event. I've just seen it. Of course, I remember the event because on that day -- or, actually, at night, at midnight, there were roadblocks in and around Banja Luka, even in front of the municipal assembly, as well as in some neighbourhoods. It has been a long time, but it's normal that I should remember. Whether or not the demands of the SOS were accepted, well, if my mind is working properly, all these documents say that the solemn declaration will be signed and that the insignia on the uniforms of police officers will be changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that one of the demands of the SOS in early April 1992 was that the JNA Banja Luka Corps be reinforced and that there should be no contemplation of any withdrawal of war equipment or manpower. Did you know that was one of their demands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was speaking about the demands of the SOS, S-O-S, I said that one of the demands -- or the reason for one of the demands was the withdrawal of the JNA from the barracks and their taking their weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the SOS was insisting as one of their conditions that the JNA not be allowed to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly their demands were, believe me. But it may have been one of their demands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that article, I think I've circled one of the boxes in the lower right under the picture, there's an article - do you find it? - entitled: Peace in the interest of all three nations. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... it's on page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's on page 6 of the English. "Replying to a reporter's question about what to do with the Security Service Centre's employees who did not sign the statement of loyalty to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia by the 6th April, Stojan Zupljanin briefly said: 'They will not be able to continue working.'" Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know about that statement of Mr. Zupljanin. But the documents I have seen here said that staff were to sign the solemn declaration. And it was normal for disciplinary proceedings to be instigated on the grounds of not signing the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then did you know that part, another part, of the demands of the SOS was the dismissal of certain Banja Luka Corps officers and public utility managers who had "voted against Yugoslavia." Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. Thank you. Let me show you one other document relating to SOS. This is tab 19; Exhibit P552. This is another article from Glas dated the 29th of April, 1992. And it's about the formation of a special police detachment to be formed at CSB Banja Luka. Mr. Zupljanin is reported as having said that: "As far as the SOS, which had been placed under jurisdiction of the CSB by a decision of the Krajina Assembly, several of those were reliable and experienced fighters who would be tested for the special detachment. Others would be assigned to the reserve police and the Krajina Territorial Defence. The SOS would thus virtually cease to exist." Is that consistent with what you know about what happened to the former members of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I heard that the special unit had been formed sometime towards the end of April in Banja Luka. I also heard that members of the military from Slavonia and reservists with some sort of war experience were included in that special unit. I heard that the commander of that special unit was a military person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who the commander was by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the special unit was a Captain Lukic from the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he then become a policeman? Because it was my understanding this special detachment was a police unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, as far as I can remember, they were not members of the police. Maybe I'm mistaken, but as far as I know, they were not members of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did they wear, the special police detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only assume because I haven't seen them. And I assume that they wore camouflage multi-coloured uniforms and that they had berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in 1992 in Banja Luka you never saw the special police detachment or any members of the special police detachment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see them, but I heard. Maybe I should give a short introduction in relation to this event that I did not witness, myself. The Security Services Centre, both in the socialist system and today, celebrates the 13th of May as the Day of the Organs of Internal Affairs. On that day, organs of internal affairs present to the citizens their technical equipment and their achievements. They go to visit schools, high schools. Pupils from high schools come to visit them to see the vehicles, the technical equipment in the forensic department, and any equipment that has to do with the work of the police. Members of the police execute special training in order to showcase their work, such as defence from an attack with knife, or other sort of attack, and things like that. So I heard that on the 13th of May, 1992, during the special celebratory parade, members of the special unit also took part in the parade. I did not see them about the town. I don't know the exact reason anymore why I myself did not attend the parade in Banja Luka. It's a pity that I didn't. Everybody from the police was there, and they presented the weaponry that they had. Maybe some long barrels; I wouldn't know exactly what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me show, then, Exhibit P1092. This is tab 60, Prosecution binder. Let me, with the usher's assistance, hand you six pages, hard copy. Thank you. Sir, if you've have a look at the top of that page. It says it's a list of members of the Banja Luka CSB special police detachment payroll for August 1992. You see the first name there is Mirko Lukic. Is that the Lukic you told us about earlier who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know his first name. I know that he is a military man, and I know that his rank was captain and that he was called Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about number 2, Ljuban Ecim? He was a member of the Banja Luka CSB, a policeman; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing: In the building, on the premises of the Banja Luka CSB, I heard that some of the members of the Security Services Centre from the state security branch were members of the special unit. That's when I heard that Ljuban Ecim and Zdravko Samardzija went to the special unit. I see those names here on the list, and I know those people from my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you'll look at page 6, and it's -- I believe it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In English, it's page 7. If we could go to page 6 in B/C/S in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we'd see the last name is number 169, and to the bottom we see for the special-purpose detachment command, signed by, apparently, Zdravko Samardzija. And then the chief of the centre, Stojan Zupljanin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we need to go one page further in the B/C/S, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This seems to indicate to me that this special police detachment must have something to do with the police. Otherwise, why is Mr. Zupljanin signing on this payroll?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say, once again, that the special unit did not belong to the CSB. It is true that two men whom I know, Ljuban Ecim and Zdravko Samardzija, according to what I heard, went to the special unit. I also heard that some of the other people who worked there went to the special unit. However, what functions they had, I wouldn't know. And I also don't know that they were members of the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll accept that you don't know that. Let me now turn to -- I'll come back to the special police later, but let me turn now to some questions about communications. I think I can do one or two here. Let me show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- Witness, before we move on to something else, could I just ask you to clarify your last answer to the Prosecutor. Because this has some importance to the trial to establish, if possible, what the affiliation was between the special unit and the CSB. Now, you have testified several times that you knew that they were not a part of the CSB, and yet, in your last answer, you - let me see if I can get it back on the screen - you say that you didn't know whether they were members of the Banja Luka CSB. So there's a difference between knowing that they were not and not knowing if they were. So which is it? What do you base your assertion that the special unit had nothing to do with the police? What is that based on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it was a wordplay again. I heard that special police had been established. I did not know that they belonged to the Security Services Centre. I heard that some of the members of the Security Services Centre, or the State Security Service, went to the special unit, as well as some other employees. Having seen the list, I gave you the example of Mr. Ecim and Mr. Samardzija, whom I know personally from my work. Now, when they went and what their functions were, I don't know even today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. But if the interpretation was correct of what you just told me in your answer, you seem, yourself, to accept that the unit was called the special police unit. Because that is what you just called it. So it would seem to me that a special police unit must, somehow, be a part of the police in the area. So I ask you again: On which basis do you assert that the special police unit had no affiliations with the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my terminology is such that we call a special unit a unit that could belong to the military or to the police or maybe even to some other organisational formations. So when I say "special unit," I'm not claiming that that unit belonged to the Security Services Centre. I know that it was established. I know that it existed. I know that some of our workers went to work there. But to say that it was part of the Security Services Centre, I have to say that I've never seen them except the parade on the 13th of May, 1992 -- excuse me, I haven't even seen them then. I only heard that they took part in the parade on the 13th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So am I to conclude that the basis on which you assert that the special unit had nothing to do with the CSB is only that you never saw them in Banja Luka? Is this correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my personal opinion. But I'm sure that I would have heard from other members at the time that this special unit belonged to the Security Services Centre. As far as I know from my conversations with my colleagues, I haven't seen them. Believe it or not, I haven't seen them even in the Banja Luka town. There were stories about them being sent to the battle-fields in Kupres, Doboj, and other places. That's what I know about the special unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But that last piece of information that you have just offered, namely, that they were send to the battle-fields in Kupres and Doboj and other places, that does not exclude, does it, that they could have been, or were, in fact, a part of the police force in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I can say that with certainty I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. I think this is as far as we'll get with this. Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just one moment. Mr. Witness, just to clarify this: Judge Harhoff asked you -- said to you that you told in -- in your answer you seem, yourself, to accept that the unit was called the special police unit. And then he asked you a question, and you started answering -- answering it; and, as from then, you don't speak about the special police unit anymore -- you speak about -- you talk about special unit. Is there a purpose in this restriction? Was it the police unit, whether it was CSB Banja Luka or not, or don't you even know that? So my question is: Can we agree on the term "special police unit," or do you only accept the term "special unit" of whatever else it would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept the word "the specials," or "special unit." And if I said "special police," well, look at the list. It says "list of the members of the special police." The word that I normally use is "the specials." Whether they were part of the Security Services Centre, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But then I understand you accept that the specials were police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What -- what else were they, then, in your opinion? Were they military or paramilitary? What were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, in my opinion, if a captain, a military person, was appointed as their commander, then, in my opinion, this unit, "the specials," were part of the military, regardless of the fact that I see the name of Ljuban Ecim here on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's been a long time, but I don't remember if you answered my question, though, about if they're not police, why is -- why is Mr. Zupljanin signing off on this document that purports to be a payroll?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I really, really do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I'll accept that. Let me show you some more documents involving references to special police, or special police detachment, or special purposes detachment, of CSB Banja Luka. And the first one is P567. Tab 27 in the Prosecution's binder. I can hand you a hard copy. It's two pages, with the usher's assistance. I'll tell you, it's dated the 21st of May, 1992, and it's from -- on the back page you'll see it's from Chief Dragomir Kutlija in Bosanski Novi SJB, addressed to the CSB Banja Luka, to the command of the special purposes detachment, and to Ljubomir Ecim personally. And basically you'll see it's a complaint about some of the actions of a special unit of the CSB regarding their activities in assisting with searching some areas in Bosanski Novi looking for weapons and explosives. And the second paragraph says: "On the 15th of May, 1992, the leading team of Bosanski Novi SJB, including police inspector ... Skondric, sent the special unit of the CSB in a BOV, armoured fighting vehicle, and a Pinzgauer to search the Muslim part of Bosanska Kostajnica." And as you see, the police chief at Novi is sending this complaint to Ecim and to the command of the special purposes detachment in CSB Banja Luka. Doesn't that suggest to you that that unit was related to the police in CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion - and I emphasise "my opinion" - this document does not show that the specials were part of the Banja Luka Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it not indicate that they must have been at least some time located there or picked up mail there, because it's addressed to CSB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, this document was sent to Ljuban Ecim. I told you that he was one of the two colleagues for whom I heard that they went to the specials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you another one that's maybe a little closer to town. This is tab 40 in the Prosecution binder; Exhibit P1081. And, again, with assistance from the usher, I can hand you a hard copy. Witness, you'll see in a minute this is dated the 4th of June, 1992, and you'll see on the back, at the bottom, it's apparently from Vladimir Tutus, chief of the SJB in Banja Luka. You know who he was; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the front page it's addressed to the Serbian MUP, I guess that's the headquarters, and to Banja Luka CSB chief, Mr. Zupljanin. And it's information about a conflict between members of the Banja Luka CSB special detachment and the Banja Luka SJB Budzak, police station, police officers in front of a couple of catering facilities. Did you know about this? Did you hear about this in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time that I hear about this event and the first time that I see this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's the bottom of your page one or the top of your page two. There's a paragraph that begins, in my English translation, saying: "The behaviour of the special detachment members is contrary to the prescribed norms and regulations for employees of internal affairs organs, which is visible in their arrogant and violent behaviour, their evasion of legal provisions of the Banja Luka CJB police officers, and even in the commission of criminal acts which are being officially prosecuted." Does that not suggest that these are policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read the document. And I can tell you I am seeing it for the first time. This is the first time I hear of this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. But do you agree with me: The way that Chief Tutus has written that it suggests that those guys were members of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, it says here that they were in camouflage uniforms with police insignia. In one part of the text, you can even see that they are described as wearing partly -- parts of uniform; whereas, other parts were civilian. Some vehicles are specified, as well as police registration plates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you agree that Mr. Tutus apparently thought they were members of the police, because, otherwise, why would he direct this complaint to the MUP headquarters and to CSB chief, Mr. Zupljanin, and not to the military or the TO or the Crisis Staff or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know what, Mr. Prosecutor, such events, such illegal conduct directed against citizens is something that we could find several examples of in the town of Banja Luka. I may have said already that many members of the army, reservists, members of different groups who were wearing particular clothes, who were armed, sporting different kinds of uniforms, such as blue ones, camouflage ones, wearing different insignia on their caps or uniforms, well, there was a lot of that. Perhaps this information was sent to the chief of the centre to notify him of such events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you another one then. Tab 42, Exhibit P1082. I'll just have you look at this one on the screen; it's only one page. Okay. This is an Official Note compiled by Nikola Tanasic and Sinisa Ponorac about a Svetko Makivic, and apparently they stopped him at 1.30 in the morning on that day. And when he was asked about why he was out after curfew, he said it didn't apply to him because he was a MUP special forces member on his way back from the front in Kotor Varos. And you see, further on, he said, "Call Stojan Zupljanin or Kesic for me so I can talk to them. Who are you to stop me?" And near the next -- the next-to-the-last paragraph, they mentioned that they told him to go to Banja Luka MUP, which he did, and then the duty officer Miladic telephoned and verified that the individual in question indeed was a member of the special unit. Now, that reference to the duty officer, I take it, refers to a duty officer in the police; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Concerning this Official Note, it was drafted by the members of the police. They reported on having stopped Svetko Makivic at a particular location. It indicates that he was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where does it indicate that he was a member of the army. It says a military police identification card. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The military police. It says he was a member of the military police. And he said that police employees could exercise no control over him. He basically belittled them, saying he didn't need any police passes of sorts. In the penultimate paragraph --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- it is stated that the duty operations officer was Miladic. In the job classification, he was a member of the military police. And it turns out that these policemen notified the duty operations officer in the police. That is my opinion, and this is my conclusion, based on the Official Note.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Miladic, the duty officer, was a policeman or a military person; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, indeed, Mr. Makivic was a military policeman, does that suggest the possibility to you that the special police detachment was actually a joint unit, made up of both police and military personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I said I heard around town that they were in the specials and that they included both army members and some employees of the CSB who had joined the specials, who may have been members of the TO. I really can't say anything else. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm passed the time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have the previous page of the document back on the screen for a moment, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we go into closed session for the witness to be escorted out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, next I'd like to show you Exhibit P1084. This is tab 44 in the Prosecution's binder. This is an Official Note relating to an event on the 19th of June, 1992, regarding an individual named Gojko Racic, a member of the reserve, that is, the special police detachment. I don't know, can you read that on the screen? Do you want to have a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me know when you're ready to go to the second page. There's just a paragraph on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you -- well, I'm sorry, I have a question that I probably should go into private session to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see this is an information dated 24 June 1992 to the CSB chief. That would have been Mr. Zupljanin. And it's from Mr. Tutus, chief of the SJB in Banja Luka. If you want to read the whole thing, let me know when you're done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'll see Chief Tutus is informing Mr. Zupljanin about some of the problems [indiscernible] concerned negative behaviour by Banja Luka CSB special police detachment members. And we see a reference to a couple that we already talked about. And in the last two paragraphs, Chief Tutus says he's attached information and Official Notes about these events, and notes that they've already sent a large number of such notes between the 22nd of May and the 19th of June. And then he reminds Chief Zupljanin about some of his previous dispatches, apparently, which set forth Zupljanin's determination to have the service function in accordance with the rules on the work of organs of the interior and the rules of the conduct of their employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, those aren't on my list, but those dispatches, 11-154 of 29 May, is -- and the other one, are Exhibits 1D85 and P1007, I believe, in evidence. So does that not suggest that at least some of these individuals were members of the Department of the Interior, because why else reference the rules on conduct of employees of the Department of Interior, or the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I told you about my knowledge concerning the specials. I told you what I knew about the members of the specials. The events described by Mr. Tutus, the chief of the SJB, which he forwarded in this letter to the chief is something I can neither deny nor confirm. First of all, I was not a participant in these events in the field, where the competent police stations had territorial jurisdiction. Also, I am not familiar with the names and with the people who were members of the specials. I am not trying to say that these events are unimportant. I don't know who were people who participated in these events and whether they were members of the specials or not. When someone introduces himself or herself during an ID check or at the time of being brought in the station following a certain event, in my view, is insufficient to try and establish whether the particular person is a member of this or that military or paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not sure you answered my original question, though. Can you explain why the SJB chief, a policeman, is writing to his superior at the CSB, chief Mr. Zupljanin, complaining about the conduct of certain members of the special police detachment and making reference to the rules on the work of organs of the interior and the rules on conduct of those employees unless he wanted or expected the chief to do something about these individuals and their work? If these people were military personnel, why would he be writing to Mr. Zupljanin and not asking Mr. Zupljanin to contact the military and do something about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me when I say I don't know why. The best person to ask would be Mr. Tutus, the SJB chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... well, this one we're looking at right --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one we're looking at right now, P1088, one of the individuals, Svetko Makivic, appears on the list of special police detachment people that we looked at, the payroll document P1092, before, as does Gojko Racic. Do you take my word for that or do I need to show you that document again? Mr. Makivic is at number 112; Mr. Gojko Racic is at number 114. I can bring up the document if you need. I see you have a hard copy. Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this the list?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You see number 14, Mr. Racic, Gojko; and number 112 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... and number 112, Mr. Makivic, Svetko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Makinic. Makinic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Svetko. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go on to something else. I need your help in understanding the chronology on the next set of three or four documents. And I'll show you the first one I have in chronological order, but I'm not sure about the chronology. Exhibit P1091 is dated the 20th of July. It's at tab 56 of the Prosecution's binder. And you can look at this on the screen, I think. It's just one page. Dated the 20th of July, 1992, to the Banja Luka SJB from CSB Banja Luka. Stojan Zupljanin's typed signature, typed name, but it appears it's signed by someone else for him, and I don't know who that was. But this dispatch says: "The security information indicates that the security situation in Banja Luka could be disturbed due to the arrest of Miroslav Dragojevic and Ljubomir Jokic. It is necessary that you release these individuals from detention and inform them to report to Banja Luka SJB tomorrow ... for further operative steps, if necessary. In other words, escort them to the ... basic court... judge. If ... they [sic] fail to report, we'll consider their further stay in the Banja Luka CSB special police detachment." Did you know anything about this event or those two individuals, Mr. Jokic and Mr. Dragojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the names Miroslav Dragojevic and the other man you mentioned, Ljubomir Jokic, they don't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall hearing anything about this incident where Chief Zupljanin directed the SJB Banja Luka to release these two men who had been detained? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragojevic and Jokic, well, there seems to be an event far in the back of my mind. As for what you say that he instructed them to release the men, well, under the law, irrespective of who is involved and what the event is, they can only keep people in custody for three days. There's a further instruction which says that they should brought before an investigating magistrate who was to decide whether their custody ought to be extended or whether they should be released. It doesn't say here that they should be released immediately. As for the events in question, I seem to remember that one event included trying to set free some army members from jail. I can't be certain. I seem to have seen -- I -- it seems that I had seen that in some documents. I believe they wanted to have them released and threatened with force. In any case, Chief Zupljanin did not sign this. In my view, these people were to be taken before an investigative magistrate at the basic court, and it was up to him to undertake further measures, such as extended custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But looking at this document, you don't know whether they'd been in detention for 12 hours or two days or three days; right? You can't tell by looking at this when they were originally detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you still have that list of detachment members, Exhibit P1092. I would ask to you look at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... 45 and 54, and you'll see the names of Mr. Jokic and Mr. Dragojevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They are on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now turn, if you will with me, to Exhibit P584. This is tab number 57. This will be up on the screen for you in a moment, Witness. This document is dated the 21st of July, to Banja Luka CSB and to the MUP, from Zoran Josic, chief of department. What department was he the chief of; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the chief of the general crime department, as far as I recall. I stand to be corrected, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this document he's reporting about some armed men who came to a house in Banja Luka and carried out an attack, shooting at one person as he was running away. And that after that event, on the night of the 20th of July, neighbours found an identity card of a certain person who apparently was a member of the special police detachment. And the chief is reporting that the criminal report was filed against that Boskan, the person whose identity card was found, Miroslav Dragojevic, and Ljubomir Jokic, the two individuals we were looking at in the previous document, and another Dragojevic. Now, let me take you to the next document in this related series. It's tab 58, Exhibit P585. This is also the 21st of July, from Mr. Josic, to the chief of CSB and to the Serbian MUP for information, indicating that a criminal report had been filed against Miroslav Dragojevic, Ljubomir Jokic, and those other two I named earlier. Near the bottom of your page --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess we need to go to page 2 in the B/C/S and page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the chief is saying: As we informed you, these men were arrested, I guess, on the 19th, and detention for three days was set up against them. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And lastly, related to this, let me show you tab 59, Exhibit P586, and I'll give you a hard copy of this document. This is another newspaper article from Glas. This one's dated the 23rd of July, 1992. The heading is: Who decides on releases? And you'll see on the left column, the second paragraph, right above the box, about honest boys. It says: It all began when Ljubomir Jokic and Miroslav Dragojevic, members of a special operations unit, were stopped at a check-point and their car was confiscated from them. They were both immediately arrested. Reading that now, does that refresh your memory a little bit about this event and these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's say I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2 in the English. The story goes on, and it talks about some comment by Ljuban Ecim. It says that on the initiative of Predrag Kojic, the commander of the unit to which Dragojevic and Jokic had belonged in the special operations unit, wanted an explanation about why those two had been arrested and why they hadn't been informed. The story goes on to report that the command appealed to Mr. Radic and Mr. Brdjanin and Dr. Vukic to insist on the release of those men but Chief Tutus refused the request. And it reports that after that Mr. Zupljanin sent a dispatch -- well, it says Zupljanin and Djuro Bulic wrote and sent a dispatch to the police station asking for the men to be released. But apparently when Tutus heard about that, he came, had a discussion with Mr. Kojic, refused to honour that direction or request from Mr. Zupljanin, and basically throwing Mr. Kojic out of his office. So then members of the special unit went to the prison and forcibly released their comrades. Does that refresh your memory about what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said that, yes, I do remember it, but it's in a haze. The two accused were put in detention pursuant to the decision of the investigative magistrate, and their detention was extended. And if we read this against that dispatch, that Mr. Zupljanin did not sign the order to -- for them to be taken to the investigative judge to extend their detention, then, clearly, if their detention is not extended and if they are brought to the interview on the following day or whenever, that makes me conclude that the investigative magistrate did extend their detention. And they were taken to the Tunjice facility, detention facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if you see at the end of the article, Mr. -- oh, I'm sorry, let me ask you this question: Did you know who Mr. Kojic was, Predrag Kojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question related to the special unit before I move on to another topic. Exhibit P1096. It's tab 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 31st of December, 1992, to the police brigade command, apparently, from Mr. Zupljanin, or at least his typed signature. It's an order appointing Ljuban Ecim as commander of the 1st Battalion and Zdravko Samardzija as assistant battalion commander and Nenad Kajkut as commander of the 1st Company in the 1st Battalion. Do you know anything about this? Why would Mr. Zupljanin, as chief of the CSB, be ordering the appointment of these individuals? Is the police brigade a police unit or a military unit; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you, Mr. Prosecutor, all that I know about the specials. I see this order in front of me. It's an order on appointment. But I haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm assuming, because there's an order to make Mr. Ecim a commander, that Mr. Zupljanin didn't have any problems with Mr. Ecim's conduct during the earlier part of the year, 1992, or he wouldn't be putting him in such a position; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I don't know. I wouldn't necessarily agree with you, because Ljuban Ecim worked for national security. And I see here the name of Zdravko Samardzija. I've already stated that I knew them. I am not inclined to agree with your assertion. That's my opinion, anyway.
